# Ball-body convexity for inverse-power-concave densities

This is a self-contained ordinary continuous lemma. It does not assert a
mixed-integer projective change of measure or construct an OC center.

## Theorem

Let r>=1 be an integer and beta>=r+1. Let f be a nonnegative integrable
density on R^r with 0<integral f<infinity and full-dimensional positive
support. Suppose the extended function

    g(x)=f(x)^(-1/beta) where f(x)>0,
    g(x)=infinity      where f(x)=0

is convex. Values f=infinity, if initially allowed, are excluded by the
argument below. Fix ANY interior point y of the positive support.
Then the radial body with

    rho_y(v)^r=r integral_0^infinity t^(r-1) f(y+t v)dt,
           |v|=1,

is a convex body. Its volume is integral f, and for every through-origin
closed halfspace H,

    vol_r(B_y intersect H)=integral_(y+H) f.             (1)

There is no mode, centroid, symmetry, stationarity, or deepest-point
hypothesis on y. The exponent threshold beta>=r+1 is retained exactly.

## 1. Global bounds from integrability

Translate y to 0. The finite convex function g is continuous on the
interior of its effective domain. Choose delta>0 and A>0 such that
the ball B(0,delta) is in that interior and g<=A on it. The density is
bounded below there by A^(-beta).

Let x be any positive-support point and write epsilon=g(x). First suppose
0<epsilon<=A, and put a=epsilon/A. For every v in B(0,delta), convexity
gives

    g((1-a)x+a v)<=(1-a)epsilon+a A<=2epsilon.

The image of this ball has volume a^r times its original volume. Thus,
writing M=integral f and omega_r for the unit-ball volume,

    M>=omega_r delta^r epsilon^(r-beta)/(2^beta A^r).

Because beta>r, this bounds epsilon away from zero by a constant independent
of x. Points with epsilon>A already obey a positive lower bound. If
g(x)=0 were allowed, use any a>0 in the same mixture: its mass is at least
omega_r delta^r A^(-beta) a^(r-beta), which tends to infinity as a tends
to zero. This contradicts integrability. Hence g is bounded below by one
positive constant on its effective domain and f is globally bounded above.

The convex sublevel set {g<=2g(0)} contains a neighborhood of 0 and must
be bounded. Otherwise its convex hull with a fixed interior ball contains
cones of arbitrarily large volume, while f is bounded below on that
sublevel set by (2g(0))^(-beta), contradicting integrability. Choose R so
that the sublevel lies in the open radius-R ball. For any positive-support
x with |x|>R, the point Rx/|x| lies in the interior of the support and

    2g(0)<g(Rx/|x|)
       <=(1-R/|x|)g(0)+(R/|x|)g(x).

Thus g(x)>g(0)+(g(0)/R)|x|. Together with the global positive lower bound,
this gives constants C,c>0 with

    f(x)<=C(1+|x|)^(-beta) for all x,
    f(x)>=c              on a ball about 0.             (2)

These bounds imply positive finite, uniformly bounded above and below
radial integrals on the unit sphere. The upper radial majorant is
integrable because beta>r.

## 2. The exact quantile/Hölder inequality

For x!=0 define

    I(x)=integral_0^infinity t^(r-1)f(tx)dt,
    Q(x)=I(x)^(-1/r),       Q(0)=0.

Then I(cx)=c^(-r)I(x) for c>0. To prove convexity of the unit sublevel
of Q, take x,y with I(x)=I(y)=1 and 0<lambda<1. Set
z=lambda x+(1-lambda)y. If z=0 there is nothing to prove.

The radial densities a^(r-1)f(ax) and b^(r-1)f(by) each integrate to one.
On each ray their positive set is an interval starting at 0, and the
density is positive and continuous before its endpoint. Its increasing
quantile is consequently C^1 on (0,1). Denote the two quantiles by
r_1(u),r_2(u); then

    r_1'=1/[r_1^(r-1)f(r_1 x)],
    r_2'=1/[r_2^(r-1)f(r_2 y)].

Define

    t=(lambda/r_1+(1-lambda)/r_2)^(-1),
    a=lambda t/r_1,        b=(1-lambda)t/r_2.

Then a,b>0, a+b=1, and

    tz=a r_1 x+b r_2 y,       t=a r_1+b r_2.

Put X=g(r_1 x), Y=g(r_2 y). Convexity gives
f(tz)>=(aX+bY)^(-beta). Differentiation yields

    t'=t[aX^beta/r_1^r+bY^beta/r_2^r]>0.

Weighted Hölder, with exponents beta and beta/(beta-1), gives

    (aX+bY)^beta
      <=[aX^beta/r_1^r+bY^beta/r_2^r]
         [a r_1^(r/(beta-1))+b r_2^(r/(beta-1))]^(beta-1).

Since r/(beta-1)<=1, concavity of this power and t=a r_1+b r_2 show

    [a r_1^(r/(beta-1))+b r_2^(r/(beta-1))]^(beta-1)<=t^r.

Combining the last three displays proves the pointwise inequality

    t^(r-1) f(tz)t' >=1.                                (3)

This retains the critical case beta=r+1, where the final concave-power
step is an equality. No even-series argument or unproved radial
rearrangement is used.

As u increases from 0 to 1, t increases from 0 to some T<=infinity.
Changing variables in (3) gives

    I(z)>=integral_0^T t^(r-1)f(tz)dt>=1.

Thus the segment between any two radial boundary points is in the unit
sublevel. Positive homogeneity makes the sublevel star-shaped; any convex
combination of two arbitrary points is a radial contraction of a convex
combination of their boundary points. This proves its convexity.

## 3. Compactness, continuity, and cap preservation

If unit directions v_j tend to v, then f(t v_j) tends to f(t v) for almost
every t>0. Indeed, a ray from an interior point has at most one finite
boundary point of the convex support. Before it f is continuous, and
beyond it points are outside the support closure. Its single boundary
value has no effect on the radial integral. The uniform integrable
majorant (2) permits dominated convergence. Hence I is continuous on
the sphere. Its positive uniform radial bounds make the unit sublevel
of Q a compact convex body containing a ball about 0.

Multiplying its radial function by r^(1/r) gives precisely B_y. Polar
integration proves its volume and every through-origin cap identity (1).
The boundaries of the halfspaces have Lebesgue measure zero for f and
ordinary volume zero for B_y, so the identities retain closed halfspaces
without a boundary-mass substitution.

Translation back to the arbitrary interior point y completes the proof.

## Scope for the current three-cap route

For r=2 this theorem applies at beta=3 to densities whose inverse cube
root is convex. Combined with the already proved planar uniform-body
overlap theorem, it transfers the coefficient 3/4 to concurrent triples
about any interior positive point of such a density. Threshold tightening
and the two-cap boundary reduction must still be justified for a particular
cover; the lemma itself asserts only (1) and convexity.

In particular this proof does not identify the density of a projective
image or establish its inverse-power concavity. Those are separate
change-of-variables and marginal-concavity obligations.
